title: Which of these six statements of proportion are true?
description: Six statements, each saying two ratios are equal, are tested by reducing both ratios to the simplest form. The ones whose simplest forms match are true, and the rest are false.
teaching_notes: One idea: a statement of proportion is true when both ratios have the same simplest form. Watch for students who swap the order of the terms.

source: Figure it Out (ratios and proportions, question 1)
video_script.why: The child applies the simplest form test to six statements, including ones with the terms swapped.
video_script.substitution: Reduce both ratios of each statement by their highest common factor and compare.
video_script.anchor: the six statements written on the board, each joining two ratios with ::
video_script.payoff_line: The first, fourth and sixth statements are true.

final_answer.spoken: the first, fourth and sixth statements are true

maths_rules: (ii) 8 : 3 :: 24 : 6: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 6 ÷ 6 = 1, so 24 : 6 is 4 : 1; 8 : 3 is already in simplest form, false
(iii) 7 : 12 :: 12 : 7: both are already in simplest form and the terms are in a different order, false
check of the true ones by multiplying across: 4 × 21 = 84 = 7 × 12; 21 × 10 = 210 = 6 × 35; 24 × 3 = 72 = 8 × 9
video_script.design: One idea: the same simplest form means a true statement. Uses the simplest form test of the solved example. The six statements stay for the whole video.

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.six: the six statements are written in two columns
marks.ask: the words true or false? appear beside each statement

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about six statements.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Each statement says that two ratios are equal.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which of the six statements are true?

beats.on_screen: the six statements hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a ratio with an arrow ÷ highest common factor giving the simplest form; two equal simplest forms joined by ::, with a tick

marks.hcf: an arrow marked ÷ highest common factor lands on each term of a ratio
marks.simple: the reduced ratio is written with the words simplest form
marks.tick: two ratios with equal simplest forms are joined by :: and a tick lands

narration: <bookmark mark='hcf'/>We use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='simple'/>Divide both terms by their highest common factor. The ratio we get is called its simplest form.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>A statement is true when both ratios have the same simplest form.

marks.a: the first two statements are written
marks.b: the next two statements are written
marks.c: the last two statements are written

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Given, the first is four to seven as twelve to twenty one. The second is eight to three as twenty four to six.
<bookmark mark='b'/>The third is seven to twelve as twelve to seven. The fourth is twenty one to six as thirty five to ten.
<bookmark mark='c'/>The fifth is twelve to eighteen as twenty eight to twelve. The sixth is twenty four to eight as nine to three.

beats.on_screen: To find: which statements are true

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which statements are true.

marks.r: 12 : 21 is written with ÷ 3 on both terms
marks.s: 4 : 7 is written and matched with the first ratio, and a tick lands

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step one, divide twelve to twenty one by three.
<bookmark mark='s'/>We get four to seven, the same as the first ratio, so the first statement is true.

marks.r: 24 : 6 is written with ÷ 6 on both terms and becomes 4 : 1
marks.s: 8 : 3 is written beside it as already in simplest form, and a cross lands

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step two, divide twenty four to six by six to get four to one.
<bookmark mark='s'/>Eight to three is already in simplest form, so the second statement is false.

beats.on_screen: (iii) 7 : 12 and 12 : 7 are in simplest form, but the order is different, false

marks.r: 7 : 12 and 12 : 7 are written side by side
marks.s: arrows show the terms in swapped places, and a cross lands

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step three, seven to twelve and twelve to seven are both in simplest form.
<bookmark mark='s'/>The terms are in a different order, so the third statement is false.

marks.s: 35 : 10 is written with ÷ 5 and becomes 7 : 2, and a tick lands

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step four, twenty one to six divided by three is seven to two.
<bookmark mark='s'/>Thirty five to ten divided by five is also seven to two, so the fourth statement is true.

marks.s: 28 : 12 is written with ÷ 4 and becomes 7 : 3, and a cross lands
marks.u: 9 : 3 is written with ÷ 3 and becomes 3 : 1, and a tick lands

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step five, twelve to eighteen divided by six is two to three.
<bookmark mark='s'/>Twenty eight to twelve divided by four is seven to three, so the fifth statement is false.
<bookmark mark='t'/>Twenty four to eight divided by eight is three to one.
<bookmark mark='u'/>Nine to three divided by three is also three to one, so the sixth statement is true.

marks.chk: the words Check: multiply across are written
marks.one: 4 × 21 = 84 and 7 × 12 = 84 are written with crossing arrows
marks.three: 24 × 3 = 72 and 8 × 9 = 72 are written, and three ticks land

narration: <bookmark mark='chk'/>Step six, check the true ones by multiplying across.
<bookmark mark='one'/>Four times twenty one is eighty four, and seven times twelve is also eighty four.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Twenty one times ten and six times thirty five are both two hundred ten.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Twenty four times three and eight times nine are both seventy two.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The first, fourth and sixth statements are true.
